# Complete supplied material

# Case-study brief and source

SYNTHETIC EVALUATION MATERIAL. Every name, event, quotation and document below is fictional. This is the complete source package. Source language: English.

## Brief

Write a journalistic customer case in American English for managers of small cultural archives. The publisher is catalog software supplier Index Lantern; the customer is Briar County Theater Archive. Approximately 250–300 words, in Markdown. Explain the customer's practical choices and qualified assessment. No author name or call to action is supplied.

## Material

Briar County Theater Archive holds donated programs, photographs, and posters from local productions. Volunteers had described new donations in separate spreadsheets. In February 2026 the archive's collection team chose to test a shared catalog for incoming donations, using Index Lantern. Existing collections were outside the pilot.

The team agreed on fields for production title, year, donor, and location. It retained a free-text note for uncertain dates. Index Lantern imported the team's spreadsheet template and provided one remote training session for five volunteers. The archive decided which descriptions to use and checked the imported records.

The archive's pilot note, dated May 6, records 47 incoming donations cataloged during the eight-week pilot. Eleven records retained uncertain dates. The note reports that volunteers could consult the same records, but contains no before-and-after time measurement, cost calculation, or assessment of public access. The archive will review the field definitions before deciding whether to move older records into the catalog.

Collection coordinator Lena Ortiz sent the following complete quotations in an email headed “Catalog pilot: notes for publication”:

- “We kept the uncertain dates visible. An empty field and an estimated year tell the next volunteer different things.”
- “Agreeing on the fields took two meetings. The import was the short part.”
- “I would use the shared catalog again for new donations. I would test the descriptions on more posters before we bring in the older collection.”

The archive supplied that email and the pilot note for this supplier-published case. These are the only correspondence and reporting materials supplied. There is no question-and-answer transcript, observation of an archive visit, or account of Ortiz's manner or emotions. The customer's assessment is limited to this pilot; no comparison with another supplier is available.

**Source-support finding and repair.**

The only missing support is for the feminine attribute embedded in **“her.”** Supporting the surrounding explanation and identifying the email’s author do not establish that attribute.

> Ortiz explained the distinction in **the email**: “We kept the uncertain dates visible. An empty field and an estimated year tell the next volunteer different things.”

All other supported claims, qualifications, certainty, and editorial choices can remain.

**Quotation and translation findings.**

All three quotation blocks reproduce the English source wording. There is no translation to assess and no concrete obstruction to reading them as idiomatic English with the supplied voice:

- “The import was the short part” retains Ortiz’s concise relative assessment.
- “Tell the next volunteer different things” retains the practical, person-centered explanation.
- The repeated “I would” retains personal judgment and the distinction between reuse for new donations and testing before older holdings enter the catalog.

The context already identifies “the fields,” “the import,” and the archive group meant by “we.” No clarification inside the quotations is needed.
